title: Ecclesiastes 12:9–14
context: The epilogue speaks about the Preacher in the third person, describing his teaching, his care with words, and the purpose of the words of the wise. Readers differ on whether these verses come from the Preacher himself or from a narrator or editor who framed the book; the notes leave that question open. The book closes with the call to fear God and keep his commandments in view of God’s judgment, which both traditions treat as shared ground.

verses.text: Further, because the Preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge. Yes, he pondered, sought out, and set in order many proverbs.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher, being wise, taught the people knowledge and set many proverbs in order. Arminian readers see wisdom shared with the people, not hoarded by an elite.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the third-person description raises the question of who wrote the epilogue. Whether the Preacher or a narrator or editor, the verse honors careful teaching.

verses.text: The Preacher sought to find out acceptable words, and that which was written blamelessly, words of truth.
verses.arminianNotes: The Preacher sought acceptable words and wrote blamelessly, words of truth. Arminian readers see care for both beauty and truth in how wisdom is expressed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the combination of pleasing words and upright truth as a model for teaching. Form and content both matter when the goal is to impart wisdom.

verses.text: The words of the wise are like goads; and like nails well fastened are words from the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.
verses.arminianNotes: The words of the wise are like goads and nails, given from one shepherd. Arminian readers see wisdom that prods and steadies, guiding people toward right paths.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that many read the one shepherd as God, the source of true wisdom, while others think of Solomon or a teacher. The identification is debated and the notes leave it open.

verses.text: Furthermore, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
verses.arminianNotes: Of making many books there is no end, and much study is a weariness of the flesh. Arminian readers see a warning against endless learning that never leads to obedience.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning as setting the words of the wise above the endless output of human writing. Study has value, but it has limits and should lead to the fear of God.

verses.text: This is the end of the matter. All has been heard. Fear God and keep his commandments; for this is the whole duty of man.
verses.arminianNotes: Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man. Arminian readers see the book’s closing call to reverent obedience, echoing Proverbs 1:7.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers share this reading: the fear of God is the foundation of wisdom, as Proverbs 1:7 also teaches. Both traditions treat the verse as the book’s summary call, not a correction of the rest.

verses.text: For God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, whether it is good, or whether it is evil.
verses.arminianNotes: God will bring every work into judgment, with every hidden thing, good or evil. Arminian readers see personal accountability for every deed; the 2 Corinthians 5:10 box discusses judgment according to deeds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Romans 2:16 speaks of God judging people’s secrets. How fully the Preacher envisioned judgment beyond death is debated, but both traditions read the verse as a solemn close.
